extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric/oratory; educated readers of classical rhetoric
extracted.subtask_description: A translated classical treatise on the nature, history, and practice of eloquence, describing what makes effective oratory and contrasting styles (Attic, Asiatic). Useful for learning standards for composing and delivering speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence consists of five branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero: 'each of the five branches of which it is said to consist, is of itself a very important art; from whence it may easily be conjectured, how great and arduous must be the profession which unites and comprehends them all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat eloquence as a composite art made of multiple distinct skills (the classical five canons). Mastery requires competence in each branch rather than relying on a single faculty; the work of an orator unites several arts into a single demanding profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion (Peitho/Suada) as the chief business
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero: 'That which the Greeks call [Peitho], (i.e. Persuasion) and which it is the chief business of an Orator to effect...' (Ennius praises an orator as the 'very marrow and quintessence of Persuasion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central evaluative goal of an oration is its persuasive effect on the audience. Style, arrangement, and delivery should serve the primary aim of producing conviction or consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosaic harmony and a certain 'metre' in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero: Isocrates 'first discovered that a certain "metre" should be observed in prose' and that the 'artificial structure and harmony of language' is an important discovery for oratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to rhythm and harmony in prose (cadence, measured sentence-length). The ear decides adequacy of cadence; craft sentences to produce pleasing, Harmonised prose rather than random or jarring rhythms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero and translator emphasize being 'clear and perspicuous' and praise orations 'expressed with greater nicety, or more clearly and poignantly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscurity and unnecessary obscurantism. Clarity of thought and expression is a core merit—convoluted ornament that impedes comprehension is a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness / mellifluent elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: Ennius calls Cethegus 'suaviloquenti' (mellifluent tongue); Cicero praises sweetness of elocution as a principal ornament of Eloquence and contrasts it with harshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pleasing, mellifluous delivery and language are virtues. Anti-pattern: harsh, barking delivery. Strive for euphony and smoothness in phrasing and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force (power) and the capacity to awe ('terrors')
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero on Pericles: 'awed by the superior force and the "terrors" of his eloquence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An orator must be capable at times of using forceful, elevated language that can awe or terrify an audience when the subject demands it. Balance force with other qualities—do not substitute mere agreeableness for necessary force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate stylistic choice (Attic vs Asiatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero contrasts Attic purity with Asiatic looseness: 'Asiatic Orators... were certainly too loose and luxuriant. But the Rhodians... more resembled the Athenians.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose style appropriate to the purpose and audience. Avoid the Asiatic excesses of loose, luxuriant, over-ornamented prose; prefer measured Attic clarity unless a different tradition is intentionally required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance versus stirring passion (agreeable vs inflaming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phalereus 'relaxed the force of Eloquence, and gave her a soft and tender air... rather pleased and entertained the Athenians, than inflamed their passions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to aim to please with elegance or to inflame and rouse passions. Pleasing elegance can charm but may fail to move; inflaming passion can persuade in different contexts. Avoid making style merely ornamental at the cost of persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and concision as conditional virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero: 'Brevity, indeed, upon some occasions, is a real excellence; but it is very far from being compatible with the general character of Eloquence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brevity when suited to purpose; recognize that full eloquence often requires extended development. Concision is a tool, not a universal rule—do not force brevity where fuller exposition is needed for persuasion or beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate judgement through study of eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero: 'Whoever, therefore, applies himself to the study of Eloquence, is at the same time improving his judgment, which is a talent equally necessary in all military operations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and practice rhetoric not merely to adorn speech but to sharpen judgment and deliberative capacity. Rhetorical training is intellectual formation as well as stylistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice, pedagogy, and composition (schools and teachers matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero recounts Isocrates as 'the School of Eloquence', Lysias as an artful composer who wrote for others, and notes the rise of writers who taught methods and rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal training, imitation of masters, and composing for practice are essential. Use teaching, composition practice, and systematic precepts to convert natural talent into reliable skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability in argument (arguing for weaker causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero cites Gorgias et al. who professed to teach 'how the worse might be made, by the force of eloquence, to appear the better cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the capacity to present different sides compellingly—useful for anticipating opposition and for persuasive flexibility—but beware ethical misuse of rhetorical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural genius versus artful method—value both
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero notes earlier ornamental effects were 'the effect rather of native genius, or of accident, than of art and observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and cultivate native talent, but systematize and refine it through art and observation. Do not rely solely on spontaneous gifts; learn method and rules to sustain excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentences governed by breath and oral delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero: 'the course of our language will necessarily be regulated by our breath, in which it is excessively disagreeable, not only to fail, but even to labour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose sentences with oral delivery in mind—appropriate length for breath and ease of speech. Avoid over-long, breathless sentences and forced constructions that make oral delivery laborious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical knowledge and orderly arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero praises Atticus's 'exact order of time' in the abridgment of Universal History for giving 'the opportunity... of beholding the history of all nations in one regular and comprehensive view.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical knowledge and coherent chronological arrangement support persuasive discourse—use ordered facts and context to strengthen arguments and provide a comprehensive view.
